title: Groupe de Galois motivique : notes manuscrites (s.d.), lettre (1965).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: a 1965 letter, probably addressed to someone who gave a talk at the Boulder 1965 conference on algebraic groups and discontinuous subgroups. The talk was on modular varieties (perhaps Shimura's or Kuga's), but the recipient is not certain.

Previous page. Fix a Q-vector space V with a symmetric or alternating form φ, G = SO(φ) (or Sp), and a homomorphism i_0 : U_R (the circle group, really S = Res_{C/R} G_m) → G_R with the parity condition on i_0(-1) and a positivity condition. The conjugacy class 𝔛 = G(R)·i_0 is a period domain, 'a direct generalization of Siegel's half-plane'. It classifies polarized Q-Hodge structures on V with fixed Hodge numbers. It carries a tautological family 𝒱, and Γ ⊂ G(Z) arithmetic gives 𝔛/Γ.

This page:
1. These orthogonal/symplectic domains are universal. A general G with i_0 maps to one of them through a faithful polarized representation, and the family 𝒱 is induced. So if the tautological family on these special 𝔛/Γ were 'algebraic' (a relative motive over the analytic space 𝔛/Γ, or over some algebraic structure on it), then every modular family on every 𝔛/Γ would be motivic.
2. Now take G(R) compact. Then Γ is finite and 𝔛 is, by Borel, a complex projective homogeneous space X = G_C/P, i.e. a flag variety. We would get a polarized motive over X.
3. A GAGA-type yoga, modelled on polarized abelian varieties, says an analytic family of motives over a projective X is algebraic. That would give a motive over X with genuinely varying Hodge structures. But X is simply connected. Granting Tate (and Hodge), the Galois/Mumford–Tate data of a motive over a simply connected base is constant, so the Hodge structures would be constant. Contradiction.
4. 'So I really do not know what to believe!'

Next page. A necessary condition for algebraicity: the Zariski closure of g·i_0(U)·g^{-1} together with Γ_0 must be all of G. He also asks whether G(Z) is Zariski-dense when G_R has no compact factors.

Modern resolution, which Grothendieck lacked in 1965:
- A family of Hodge structures coming from geometry/motives is a variation of Hodge structure. It satisfies Griffiths transversality ∇F^p ⊂ F^{p-1} ⊗ Ω^1 (Griffiths 1968).
- The tautological family on a general period domain is not transversal. It is so only when 𝔛 is Hermitian symmetric and ad∘h has Hodge types (-1,1),(0,0),(1,-1), which is Deligne's Shimura-datum axiom.
- In the compact case the tautological family on the flag variety is never a VHS (unless trivial), so there is no contradiction with Tate. The premise in step 1 is simply false outside the classical case.
- Griffiths–Robles–Toledo (2014) later showed that non-classical Γ\D are not algebraic at all.
- Bakker–Brunebarbe–Tsimerman (o-minimal GAGA, quasi-projectivity of images of period maps, c. 2018–2022) realize the 'GAGA yoga' properly, for transversal period maps.
- Borel's density theorem (1960) answers the next page's question affirmatively.
errors: The paradox rests on an implicit false premise. The tautological family of Hodge structures on a general period domain (in particular on a compact flag domain) is not a variation of Hodge structure, because it fails Griffiths transversality. It therefore cannot be motivic, and no contradiction with Tate arises. Grothendieck does not identify this; transversality was only published by Griffiths around 1968.

Calling the contradiction one 'with Tate's conjectures' is somewhat loose. The rigidity used (constancy of a motivic or l-adic family over a simply connected base) would today be derived from Deligne's theorem of the fixed part / semisimplicity, plus Mumford–Tate considerations. Tate (with Hodge) is one route, but not the essential one.

The 'GAGA yoga' (an analytic family of motives over a projective base is algebraic) is stated as heuristic. It holds for polarized VHS by Griffiths/Borel-type extension and Bakker–Brunebarbe–Tsimerman results, but only for transversal families.
Next page: the question on Zariski density of G(Z) was already answered (yes) by Borel's density theorem (1960). Grothendieck seems unaware of it.

ideas.what: Period domains 𝔛 = G(R)/centralizer of i_0 for orthogonal/symplectic groups classify polarized Hodge structures with fixed Hodge numbers, generalizing the Siegel half-space; general (G, i_0) domains are induced from these via faithful polarized representations.
ideas.modern_name: Griffiths period domains; Mumford–Tate domains; reduction of Shimura data to GSp/SO embeddings
ideas.usually_credited_to: Griffiths (1968); Mumford (1966) for Mumford–Tate groups; Deligne (1971, 1979) for Shimura data

ideas.what: Question whether the tautological Hodge family on 𝔛/Γ is motivic ('algebraic'), and a test case (G(R) compact, 𝔛 a flag variety) showing it cannot be, assuming GAGA and Tate.
ideas.modern_name: Non-motivic nature of non-classical period domains; Griffiths transversality obstruction; non-algebraicity of non-classical Γ\D

ideas.what: Rigidity: a polarized motive over a simply connected projective base has constant Hodge structure (via Tate/Galois).
ideas.modern_name: Theorem of the fixed part / rigidity of VHS; constancy of Mumford–Tate group over simply connected base

ideas.what: 'GAGA yoga': analytic families of polarized motives over algebraic bases are algebraic, modelled on polarized abelian schemes.
ideas.modern_name: Algebraicity of period maps / o-minimal GAGA; Borel extension theorem

missed.claim: Documented 1965 prehistory: Grothendieck observed that motivic families on arbitrary period domains lead to a contradiction (via the compact flag-domain case) and was left perplexed. The resolution is Griffiths transversality and Deligne's Shimura axioms. This shows the motivic Galois group programme running directly into the problem that Shimura data later solved, before transversality was published.
missed.quote: we get a contradiction with Tate's conjectures (because X is simply connected, as well known). So I really do not know what to believe!
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historically, this is an early instance of the 'non-classical period domain' phenomenon, later studied by Carlson–Toledo and Griffiths–Robles–Toledo, arising from motivic considerations. It is useful for the history of Shimura varieties and motives; it contains no new mathematics.

missed.claim: Grothendieck explicitly links a GAGA principle for families of motives with Tate/Hodge conjectures as a criterion for which locally symmetric quotients carry motivic families. This foreshadows the modern o-minimal GAGA plus Mumford–Tate approach (Bakker–Brunebarbe–Tsimerman; Griffiths–Robles–Toledo).
missed.quote: If we admit the GAGA yoga (coming from polarized abelian varieties) that such a family must also be a motive over X
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Largely realized by later work, so mainly of historical interest.

deep.surprise_reason: This is an interesting, apparently unpublished record of Grothendieck in 1965 confronting the non-motivic nature of general period domains, with the resolution (transversality, Shimura axioms) only found later by Griffiths and Deligne. The mathematics is fully superseded and he reaches no result, so it is notable only historically.
transcription_corrections: The symbol transcribed as 'V' in 'V/Γ', 'on such special type of V' and 'V = complex projective' is in the image the curly letter used for the domain (𝔛 on the previous page). Only the families are script 𝒱. So read '𝔛/Γ', 'special type of 𝔛', '𝔛/Γ = 𝔛 = complex projective homogeneous space X'.
'the V's considered above' should be '𝒱's' (the families of Hodge structures).
'over the analytic space V corresponding to X' should be 'over the analytic space 𝔛 corresponding to X'.
'Taking the case G(R) compact': the image shows G(ℝ) with a correction over the R; the struck word before 'and' is 'thus'.
